concepts.title: @SpringBootTest and Test Slices
concepts.description: @SpringBootTest boots the entire ApplicationContext for a true end-to-end test, while test slices like @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest load only the beans one specific layer needs -- a deliberate trade-off between fidelity and speed that shapes how a healthy Spring Boot test suite is structured.
learningObjectives: Explain what @SpringBootTest does and when a genuine full-context integration test is actually justified.
Explain what a test slice is and describe what @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest each load and exclude.
Explain, mechanistically, why test slices start dramatically faster than @SpringBootTest.
Predict which beans are and are not available inside a given test slice, and what happens when you autowire a bean that isn't.
Choose the appropriate test annotation -- plain unit test, a specific slice, or full @SpringBootTest -- for a given testing scenario.

sections.heading: The Cost of a Full ApplicationContext in Tests
sections.body:
`@SpringBootTest` on a test class tells Spring Boot to do exactly what it does when your application actually runs in production: build a complete `ApplicationContext`, run component scanning across your whole base package, evaluate every autoconfiguration condition, and construct every bean your application defines -- controllers, services, repositories, the works. If you set `webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT`, it goes further and starts a real embedded servlet container on an actual (randomly chosen) TCP port, so a test can fire genuine HTTP requests at it, exactly the way a real client would.

That fidelity is valuable, but it isn't free. Every bean in that graph has to be instantiated and wired, every autoconfiguration class has to run its conditional checks, and if your application talks to a real (or embedded) database, that connection has to be established too. For a small application this might take a second or two; for a real production-sized codebase with dozens of services, repositories, and autoconfigured integrations, a single `@SpringBootTest` context can take several seconds just to boot -- before the test itself has asserted anything at all. Multiply that by hundreds of test classes each demanding their own full context, and a test suite that should run in well under a minute can balloon into a ten-or-fifteen-minute slog, which is a genuine, recurring pain point in real Spring Boot codebases and the entire motivation for test slices existing at all.

sections.heading: Test Slices: Loading Only What You Need
sections.body:
A **test slice** is a specialized test annotation that boots a *deliberately restricted* subset of the full autoconfiguration and component-scanning machinery -- just enough to exercise one architectural layer in isolation, and nothing else.

`@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` loads the web layer only: `DispatcherServlet`, `HandlerMapping`, the registered `HttpMessageConverter`s (Jackson among them), `@ControllerAdvice` beans, Bean Validation support, and the one controller class you named (or every `@Controller`/`@RestController` in the base package, if you omit the argument). Critically, it does **not** perform full component scanning for `@Service` or `@Repository` beans -- if `OrderController` depends on an `OrderService`, that dependency will not be satisfied automatically, and you must supply a test double for it yourself (typically with `@MockBean`, covered later in this module). This is a deliberate restriction, not an oversight: a controller test's job is to verify routing, request/response binding, and validation -- not to also exercise a real service and a real database.

`@DataJpaTest` is the mirror image for the persistence layer: it configures an embedded, in-memory database (H2, by default, if it's on the classpath) instead of your real production datasource, scans for `@Entity` classes and Spring Data repository interfaces, and wires up a real `EntityManager` -- but registers none of your `@Service` or `@Controller` beans at all. It also wraps every test method in a transaction that is rolled back automatically at the end of that method, so tests never leak data into one another (covered in the examples below) and never need explicit cleanup code.

sections.heading: Why Slices Load Faster: Fewer Beans, and Context Caching
sections.body:
The speed difference between a slice and a full `@SpringBootTest` comes from two compounding effects. First, and most obviously, there are simply far fewer beans to construct -- a `@WebMvcTest` for one controller might build a few dozen beans; the equivalent full context for a real application might build several hundred. Fewer beans means less reflection-based construction, less dependency-graph resolution, and no attempt to establish a real (or embedded) database connection unless the slice specifically needs one.

Second, and less obviously, Spring's test framework **caches contexts across test classes**. If two test classes request an `ApplicationContext` built from the exact same configuration -- the same slice annotation, the same set of `@MockBean`s, the same active profiles -- Spring reuses the already-built context from the first test class instead of building a fresh one for the second. Because a slice's configuration is narrow and easy to keep identical across many test classes (many `@WebMvcTest` classes in the same codebase end up with an essentially identical configuration key), slices benefit from this caching far more consistently than `@SpringBootTest` classes do, where subtle differences between test classes -- a different active profile, a different set of mocked beans -- are more likely to force a brand-new context to be built each time, defeating the cache. `@DirtiesContext`, when applied, explicitly opts a test out of this caching by forcing the context to be discarded and rebuilt after that test runs -- useful when a test mutates shared singleton state in a way that would corrupt subsequent tests, but it should be used sparingly, since it directly reintroduces the startup cost the caching mechanism exists to avoid.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tool: Plain Unit Test, Slice, or Full Context
sections.body:
A healthy test suite is not made entirely of one kind of test -- it's a mix, chosen deliberately per test's actual purpose. For pure business logic with no Spring dependency at all -- a pricing calculation, a validation rule implemented as a plain method -- a plain JUnit test with `new SomeClass()` and, if needed, hand-written or Mockito-created fakes, needs no Spring context whatsoever and runs in milliseconds. For verifying that one layer's Spring-specific wiring behaves correctly -- does this controller route requests and bind JSON the way I expect? does this repository's derived query method actually produce the right SQL? -- a test slice is the right level: it exercises real Spring infrastructure for exactly the layer under test, with everything else mocked or absent. `@SpringBootTest` earns its cost specifically for true end-to-end scenarios: verifying that a request really does flow correctly from the controller, through a real service, into a real (often embedded, e.g. Testcontainers-backed) database and back out again, exactly as it would in production.

The common mistake worth naming explicitly is reaching for `@SpringBootTest` as a default habit for every single test, including ones that only ever touch one layer. It works, in the sense that the test passes -- but it quietly taxes the entire suite's runtime for no corresponding gain in what that specific test is actually verifying, and it's a cost that compounds linearly with every test class that makes the same choice. The right question to ask before reaching for `@SpringBootTest` is not 'will this work?' but 'does this specific test actually need more than one layer wired together to make its assertion meaningful?'

examples.title: @WebMvcTest: Web Layer Only, With a Mocked Service
examples.explanation: @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) restricts the context to the web layer and this one controller -- DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, Jackson's HttpMessageConverter, and validation support are all present, but no @Service or @Repository bean is component-scanned into this context at all. Because OrderController's constructor requires an OrderService, that dependency has to be supplied explicitly; @MockBean does exactly that, registering a Mockito mock of OrderService into this narrow context so the controller can still be constructed. The test itself never touches a real service or a real database -- it is entirely about verifying that a GET request to this specific URL is routed correctly and that the returned Order object is serialized to the JSON shape the test expects.

examples.title: @DataJpaTest: Persistence Layer Only, With Automatic Rollback
examples.explanation: @DataJpaTest swaps in an embedded, in-memory database instead of whatever datasource the real application would use, and registers only @Entity classes and Spring Data repository interfaces -- no @Service or @Controller beans exist in this context. TestEntityManager is a test-oriented wrapper Spring Boot provides specifically for this slice, giving convenient access to persist data directly, bypassing the repository under test so the test setup itself doesn't depend on the exact method being tested. The second test method demonstrates the automatic-rollback behavior directly: @DataJpaTest wraps every test method in its own transaction and rolls it back at the end, so the two orders persisted in the first test are gone by the time the second test runs, with no manual cleanup code required anywhere.

examples.title: @SpringBootTest With a Real Embedded Server: True End-to-End
examples.explanation: Unlike the two slice examples above, this test builds the ENTIRE application context -- every controller, service, and repository, plus a real embedded servlet container listening on an actual randomly-assigned port -- and TestRestTemplate fires genuine HTTP requests at it, exactly as an external client would. This is the only one of the three examples that actually proves the controller, service, and repository correctly cooperate end-to-end, including real HTTP serialization on both sides of the wire; it's also, by a wide margin, the slowest of the three to start, since nothing here is restricted or mocked. Reaching for this style for every test in a suite -- rather than reserving it for genuine cross-layer scenarios -- is exactly the habit that makes large Spring Boot test suites slow.

misconceptions.description: @WebMvcTest loads the entire application, just with a mock server instead of a real one listening on a port.
misconceptions.clarification: @WebMvcTest restricts which BEANS get loaded, not just how the server is exposed -- it deliberately excludes @Service and @Repository component scanning entirely, alongside most other autoconfiguration unrelated to the web layer. A controller's non-web dependencies (typically a service) are simply absent from this context unless you explicitly supply them, most commonly via @MockBean. This is fundamentally different from @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = MOCK), which DOES build the full application context -- every bean your app defines -- but serves requests through a mock servlet environment instead of a real network port. The two axes (which beans are loaded, and whether a real socket is opened) are independent of each other.

misconceptions.description: Since @DataJpaTest starts a real repository bean backed by a real EntityManager, it must be exercising the exact same database and configuration the production application uses.
misconceptions.clarification: @DataJpaTest deliberately replaces your production datasource configuration with an embedded, in-memory database (H2 by default, when present on the classpath) purely for the duration of the test, and wraps every test method in a transaction that's rolled back automatically once the method finishes. The repository and EntityManager are genuinely real Spring Data / JPA objects performing real SQL under the hood -- but the database itself is a disposable, in-memory stand-in, not your production database or even a persistent local one, and nothing written during a test is ever actually retained afterward. This is precisely what makes @DataJpaTest fast and safe to run repeatedly with no manual cleanup.

exercises.prompt: This @WebMvcTest fails at startup with 'NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type OrderService available.' Find and fix the bug so the test can construct OrderController successfully.
hints: @WebMvcTest deliberately does NOT perform full component scanning -- does it register @Service beans like OrderService into the context at all?
@Autowired only finds a bean that already exists in the context. If no OrderService bean was ever registered here, what should happen instead of trying to autowire a real one?
You need a way to supply a stand-in OrderService so OrderController's constructor can be satisfied, without loading the real service bean at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @WebMvcTest scans and registers only the web layer -- @Controller/@RestController beans, plus supporting web infrastructure -- and explicitly excludes @Service and @Repository beans from component scanning. Because no OrderService bean is ever registered in this context, @Autowired has nothing to find and the context fails to start while trying to construct OrderController, whose constructor demands an OrderService. Replacing @Autowired with @MockBean fixes this correctly: rather than looking for an existing bean, @MockBean creates a Mockito mock and registers IT as the OrderService bean in this test's context, which satisfies OrderController's constructor while keeping the real service (and everything it would otherwise depend on) out of the picture entirely.

exercises.prompt: Given this @DataJpaTest class with two test methods, what does each assertion produce, and why doesn't the second test see the order persisted by the first?
hints: @DataJpaTest wraps every test method in its own transaction by default -- what happens to that transaction once the test method finishes?
JUnit does not guarantee these two methods run in the same database state on purpose -- what mechanism specifically resets things between them?
Neither test method contains any manual cleanup code (no @AfterEach deleting rows) -- so the reset has to be happening automatically, at the transaction level.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Both assertions pass: firstTestPersistsAnItem sees count() == 1 right after persisting one item, and secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable sees count() == 0, because @DataJpaTest automatically rolls back each test method's transaction once that method completes -- the widget persisted in the first test never actually commits, so the second test starts from a genuinely empty table.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @DataJpaTest wraps every individual test method in its own database transaction, and by default rolls that transaction back automatically once the method finishes -- regardless of whether the test passed or failed. In firstTestPersistsAnItem, entityManager.persist(...) adds a row within that method's transaction, so inventoryRepository.count() correctly reports 1 while still inside that same transaction. Once the method returns, Spring's test framework rolls the transaction back, which erases that insert as if it never happened. secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable then runs in a brand new transaction with no knowledge of the first test's data at all, so count() correctly reports 0. This automatic rollback is precisely why @DataJpaTest tests can run in any order and be repeated indefinitely without ever needing explicit teardown code to reset the database between them.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best explains why a @WebMvcTest-based test suite typically starts dramatically faster than the equivalent @SpringBootTest-based suite?
options: @WebMvcTest disables Jackson's JSON serialization, so responses are returned as plain text instead, which is faster to produce.

@WebMvcTest loads a deliberately restricted set of beans (the web layer only, excluding @Service/@Repository component scanning), and its narrow, easily-repeated configuration also benefits more consistently from Spring's test-context caching.
@WebMvcTest tests run in a separate, permanently pre-warmed JVM that Spring Boot maintains between test runs.
@WebMvcTest skips Bean Validation entirely, which is the single largest cost in a typical Spring Boot context startup.
assessments.explanation: The speed advantage comes from two compounding factors: far fewer beans need to be constructed (no full component scan for services/repositories, no autoconfiguration unrelated to the web layer), and a slice's narrow, easily-kept-identical configuration is reused across test classes far more often thanks to Spring's test-context caching than a typical @SpringBootTest's configuration, which more often varies just enough between test classes to force a fresh context each time. Option A is false -- Jackson-based JSON conversion is still fully active in @WebMvcTest. Option C describes a JVM-level mechanism Spring Boot does not implement. Option D is false -- Bean Validation support is present in @WebMvcTest, and is not the dominant cost of a full context startup anyway.

assessments.prompt: A @DataJpaTest class autowires a real OrderRepository and asserts against data it persists via TestEntityManager. Which statement about this test is accurate?
options: It exercises the exact same database configuration -- URL, driver, and data -- that the production application actually connects to.

It exercises a genuine Spring Data JPA repository and EntityManager, but against a disposable, embedded, in-memory database substituted specifically for the test, with each test method's transaction rolled back automatically once it finishes.
It requires explicit cleanup code (an @AfterEach deleting rows) at the end of each test method, or later tests will see leftover data from earlier ones.
It also loads and exercises any @Service or @Controller beans that happen to depend on OrderRepository.
assessments.explanation: @DataJpaTest deliberately swaps in an embedded, in-memory database in place of the production datasource, and wraps every test method in its own transaction that's automatically rolled back afterward -- the repository and EntityManager objects themselves are genuinely real, but the database backing them is a disposable stand-in. Option A is exactly the misconception this concept calls out directly. Option C is wrong because the automatic rollback IS the cleanup mechanism -- no manual teardown code is needed. Option D is wrong -- @DataJpaTest registers only @Entity classes and repository interfaces, explicitly excluding @Service and @Controller beans from its restricted context.

assessments.prompt: A test class is annotated @DirtiesContext, applied after a test that mutates a shared singleton bean's internal state in a way that would corrupt later tests. What is the direct effect of this annotation?
options: It marks the test as flaky so the CI pipeline automatically retries it on failure.

It forces Spring's test framework to discard the cached ApplicationContext after this test runs and build a fresh one the next time a context is needed, at the cost of reintroducing that context's full startup time.
It disables all @MockBean stubbing within this specific test class from that point forward.
It prevents the test's own transaction from being rolled back at the end of the method.
assessments.explanation: @DirtiesContext explicitly opts a test out of Spring's test-context caching by forcing the context to be discarded and rebuilt afterward -- useful specifically when a test has mutated shared singleton state in a way that would corrupt subsequent tests reusing the same cached context, but it directly reintroduces the startup cost the caching mechanism exists to avoid, which is exactly why the module recommends using it sparingly. Options A, C, and D each describe an effect @DirtiesContext does not have -- it has nothing to do with retries, mock stubbing, or transaction rollback behavior.

assessments.prompt: A class PricingCalculator has no Spring annotations at all and depends on nothing but plain Java objects passed into its constructor. According to this module's guidance on choosing a testing approach, what is the most appropriate way to test it?
options: @SpringBootTest, since every class in a Spring Boot codebase should be tested against the full application context for consistency.
A plain JUnit test that constructs PricingCalculator directly with `new`, using hand-written or Mockito-created fakes for any collaborators if needed -- no Spring context of any kind is required.
@DataJpaTest, since among Spring's test annotations it boots the fastest.
@WebMvcTest, scoped narrowly to just this one class.
assessments.explanation: The module is explicit that pure business logic with no Spring dependency at all needs no Spring context whatsoever -- a plain JUnit test with `new` and, if needed, a hand-written or Mockito-created fake, runs in milliseconds and is the most proportionate tool for this job. Option A describes exactly the habit the module names as a common mistake: reaching for @SpringBootTest as a default rather than asking whether the test actually needs more than one layer wired together. Options C and D both invoke Spring test infrastructure -- an embedded database and the web layer, respectively -- that PricingCalculator has no relationship to at all.

assessments.prompt: A teammate wants to write every single test in the codebase using @SpringBootTest 'to be safe.' Explain the trade-off they're making, and describe when a test slice or a plain unit test would be the better choice instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: @SpringBootTest builds the same full ApplicationContext the real application uses in production -- every controller, service, repository, and autoconfigured bean, plus, if configured with a real webEnvironment, an actual embedded server listening on a real port. That gives the highest possible fidelity: a test written this way genuinely exercises the whole wiring of the application, exactly as production would. But that fidelity has a real and compounding cost -- every one of those beans has to be constructed and wired for every test class that demands a distinct context configuration, and for a real-sized application that can mean several seconds of startup time per test class, which adds up linearly across a large suite into minutes of pure overhead before a single assertion has even run. 'To be safe' is a reasonable instinct, but it conflates two different things: whether a test COULD catch a bug (true of almost any test that exercises the relevant code path) and whether a test NEEDS the full wired application to make its specific assertion meaningful. A test asserting that a controller correctly routes a GET request and serializes a response as JSON doesn't need a real service or a real database behind it at all -- a @WebMvcTest with the service mocked out via @MockBean verifies exactly the same routing and serialization behavior, using only a fraction of the beans, and benefits far more reliably from Spring's test-context caching across test classes since its configuration tends to stay identical from one test class to the next. Similarly, a test asserting pure business logic with no Spring dependency at all -- a discount calculation, a formatting rule -- needs no Spring context whatsoever; a plain JUnit test with `new` and, if needed, a hand-written fake, runs in milliseconds and is trivially easy to reason about in isolation. The healthiest suite reserves @SpringBootTest for the specific, comparatively rare tests that are actually about cross-layer integration -- does a request really flow correctly from the controller through a real service into a real (or embedded) database and back -- and uses slices or plain unit tests for everything that's really only ever exercising one layer or no Spring machinery at all.

concepts.title: Testing Controllers with MockMvc
concepts.description: MockMvc simulates HTTP requests against Spring MVC's real dispatch machinery without opening an actual network socket, letting you assert on status codes, headers, and JSON response bodies with precision, at unit-test speed.
learningObjectives: Explain what MockMvc actually does and how it differs from firing real HTTP requests at a running server.
Perform a GET or POST request through MockMvc and assert on status code, content type, and JSON body fields using jsonPath.
Explain how MockMvc becomes available inside a @WebMvcTest, and how it can also be obtained in a full @SpringBootTest.
Chain multiple andExpect() assertions and explain what happens, and what gets reported, when one of them fails.
Explain why a MockMvc test still meaningfully exercises real Spring MVC infrastructure -- routing, converters, and validation -- despite never opening a socket.

sections.heading: What MockMvc Actually Does
sections.body:
`MockMvc` is a Spring test utility that simulates an HTTP request being dispatched through Spring MVC's real machinery -- `DispatcherServlet`, `HandlerMapping`, argument resolvers, `HttpMessageConverter`s, and any registered `@ExceptionHandler`s -- entirely in memory, with no actual servlet container running and no real TCP socket opened anywhere. This is a meaningfully different tool from `TestRestTemplate` or `WebTestClient`, both of which fire genuine HTTP requests at a real, running server (typically used alongside `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`, as seen in the previous concept): those tools test the whole stack including real network serialization; MockMvc tests the web layer's *logic* -- routing, binding, conversion, validation, error handling -- without paying for a real network round trip at all.

The word 'mock' here is doing something slightly different than it does in `@MockBean` or plain Mockito. It does not mean 'a fake stand-in that returns whatever you told it to.' It means 'a simulated request/response exchange that never touches a real socket' -- the request-handling code itself is entirely real.

sections.heading: Building and Performing Requests
sections.body:
A typical MockMvc test builds a request using static methods from `MockMvcRequestBuilders` (`get(...)`, `post(...)`, `put(...)`, `delete(...)`), optionally attaches a body and a `Content-Type` for write operations, calls `perform(...)`, and then chains one or more `andExpect(...)` assertions against the resulting `ResultActions`:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))
        .andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
        .andExpect(jsonPath("$.customerName").value("Amy"))
        .andExpect(jsonPath("$.items", hasSize(2)));
```

`jsonPath("$.customerName")` navigates the response body as parsed JSON, using a JSONPath expression -- `$` is the document root, `.customerName` descends into that field, `$.items[0]` would index into an array's first element, and `hasSize(2)` (a Hamcrest matcher) asserts an array's length directly rather than its contents. For a write operation, the request body is typically built by serializing a Java object with an `ObjectMapper` and attaching it explicitly:

```java
mockMvc.perform(post("/api/orders")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content(objectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)))
        .andExpect(status().isCreated());
```

sections.heading: Why It's Still a Real Test of Your Web Layer
sections.body:
It's worth being precise about exactly what 'mock' does and doesn't mean here, because it's a genuinely common point of confusion: nothing about Spring MVC's own components is replaced with a fake. The real `DispatcherServlet` dispatches the request; the real `HandlerMapping` decides which controller method matches; real argument resolvers bind `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, and `@RequestBody` parameters exactly as they would for a genuine HTTP request; the real, autoconfigured Jackson `HttpMessageConverter` performs the actual JSON serialization and deserialization; real Bean Validation runs against `@Valid`-annotated parameters; and any real `@RestControllerAdvice` you've registered handles thrown exceptions exactly as it would in production. The *only* thing that's simulated is the transport layer itself -- there is no real socket, no real servlet container thread pool, no real network latency. Everything from the moment a request 'arrives' onward is the genuine production code path.

This is precisely why a MockMvc test catches real bugs: a typo in a `@RequestMapping` path, a missing `@Valid`, a controller that returns the wrong HTTP status, a validation constraint that doesn't fire the way you expect -- all of these are caught by a MockMvc test, because the code responsible for each of them is genuinely running, not stubbed out.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls: Content-Type, JSON Path Syntax, and Assertion Failures
sections.body:
The single most common mistake when POSTing a body through MockMvc is forgetting `.contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)` on the request. Without it, Spring MVC has no declared `Content-Type` to select a message converter by, and a `@RequestBody`-annotated parameter fails to bind, typically producing a `415 Unsupported Media Type` response that has nothing to do with your actual business logic or JSON shape -- it never even got that far.

A second common source of friction is JSONPath expression mistakes: `jsonPath("$.items[0].name")` and `jsonPath("$.items[0].Name")` are not the same expression (JSON keys are case-sensitive), and asserting `jsonPath("$.items").value("mug")` against an actual JSON array produces a confusing failure, because `.value(...)` expects the path to resolve to a single scalar, not a collection -- `jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("mug")` or `jsonPath("$.items", hasItem("mug"))` are the corrections, depending on intent. When an `andExpect(...)` assertion does fail, MockMvc's failure message is deliberately verbose on purpose -- it includes the full request that was sent and the full response that came back, which is worth reading in full rather than skimming, since the actual response body very often reveals the real cause (a validation error you didn't expect, an exception message from an unhandled `@ExceptionHandler` gap) far faster than guessing from the assertion alone.

examples.title: A GET Request With Nested jsonPath Assertions
examples.explanation: The test stubs orderService.findById(1L) to return a fully-populated Order, then sends a real GET request through DispatcherServlet using MockMvc. The chained andExpect() calls assert against the response in increasing detail: an overall 200 status, the correct Content-Type header (confirming Jackson's converter was actually selected), a top-level field value, an array's length, and a specific array element's value. If any single assertion in the chain fails, MockMvc stops there and reports that specific failure along with the full response body, making it straightforward to see exactly what the controller actually returned versus what was expected.

examples.title: A POST Request Triggering Validation, Asserting on the Error Body
examples.explanation: This test never calls orderService.create(...) with a stubbed return value, because the point of the test is that the request should be rejected before the controller's own logic (and therefore the service) is ever reached at all -- @Valid triggers Bean Validation against the deserialized CreateOrderRequest, a blank customerName fails @NotBlank, and the @RestControllerAdvice's MethodArgumentNotValidException handler produces the 400 with a structured error body, exactly as covered in the Building REST APIs module. verifyNoInteractions(orderService) makes that expectation explicit and would fail the test if the controller somehow called the service anyway, catching a regression that jsonPath assertions on the response alone might not.

examples.title: Verifying a Service Was Called With the Right Arguments
examples.explanation: Rather than only inspecting the HTTP response, this test also verifies that OrderController correctly deserialized the incoming JSON and passed a correctly-populated CreateOrderRequest object into orderService.create(...). argThat(...) lets the verification inspect the actual argument's fields rather than requiring exact object equality, which matters here since CreateOrderRequest may not override equals(). This combination -- asserting the HTTP-facing response AND verifying the collaborator was invoked correctly -- is a common, thorough pattern for controller tests: the response assertions confirm what the client sees, and the verify() confirms the controller did the right thing internally to produce it.

misconceptions.description: Because MockMvc doesn't open a real network socket, it doesn't really test Spring's request-handling logic -- it's closer to calling the controller method directly.
misconceptions.clarification: MockMvc dispatches the simulated request through the exact same DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, argument resolvers, HttpMessageConverters, and @ExceptionHandler machinery that a real HTTP request would go through -- the only thing that's simulated is the transport (no real socket, no real servlet container). Calling a controller method directly with new OrderController(mockService).getOrder(1L) would bypass ALL of that -- no routing, no @PathVariable binding, no JSON conversion, no validation, no exception translation -- and would fail to catch an entire class of real bugs (a wrong mapping path, a missing @Valid, a broken @ExceptionHandler) that a MockMvc test catches precisely because it exercises the real dispatch pipeline.

misconceptions.description: You can only use MockMvc inside a @WebMvcTest -- getting a MockMvc instance requires that specific slice.
misconceptions.clarification: @WebMvcTest is simply the most common way to get an autowired MockMvc instance, because it's pre-configured and ready to use out of the box. MockMvc is also available inside a full @SpringBootTest configured with webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.MOCK (the default web environment, in fact, when webEnvironment isn't specified at all) by autowiring it the same way. It can even be constructed manually outside of any Spring test context at all, via MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(new OrderController(fakeService)).build(), for a lighter-weight test that skips Spring's context entirely and wires up just the one controller by hand.

exercises.prompt: This test fails with status 415 (Unsupported Media Type) instead of the expected 201, even though the JSON payload itself is well-formed and matches CreateOrderRequest exactly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Spring MVC needs to know what format the request body is in before it can pick an HttpMessageConverter to read it -- where does that information normally come from?
Compare this request-building chain to one that successfully posts JSON elsewhere in the test suite -- what call is present there but missing here?
The fix does not involve the JSON content at all -- it involves declaring the request's Content-Type header explicitly on the MockMvc request builder.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original request supplies a body via .content(...) but never declares a Content-Type at all. Without a declared Content-Type, Spring MVC has no way to select which HttpMessageConverter should be responsible for reading that body, and the @RequestBody parameter resolution fails before the controller's own logic (and therefore before any JSON structure or validation issue) is ever considered -- producing 415 Unsupported Media Type, a transport-level rejection, not a data problem. Adding .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) declares the body's format explicitly, letting Spring MVC correctly select the Jackson-based JSON converter, after which deserialization and the rest of the request proceeds normally.

exercises.prompt: Write a @WebMvcTest for a GET /api/products/{id} endpoint. ProductController depends on a ProductService with a method findById(Long) that returns a Product(Long id, String name, BigDecimal price). Stub the service to return a Product with id=5, name="Desk Lamp", price=29.99, then assert the response is 200 OK with the correct name and price in the JSON body.
hints: Use given(productService.findById(5L)).willReturn(...) (BDDMockito style) or when(...).thenReturn(...) to stub the mocked service before performing the request.
jsonPath("$.price") will resolve to a numeric JSON value -- compare it with .value(29.99) (a Double/number literal), not a String.
Don't forget the leading $ and dot syntax for jsonPath expressions -- $.name and $.price for top-level fields on the response object.
exercises.solutionExplanation: given(productService.findById(5L)).willReturn(...) stubs the mocked ProductService so that, when the controller calls it with 5L (extracted from the {id} path variable in the request), it returns a fully-populated Product rather than null or a default mock response. mockMvc.perform(get("/api/products/5")) sends the simulated request through the real DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping, which routes it to ProductController's handler method, binds 5 from the path to the Long parameter, and calls the (mocked) service. The response, serialized by the real Jackson converter, is then asserted field by field with jsonPath -- confirming both the status code and that the controller correctly passed the service's data through into the JSON response body.

assessments.prompt: What is the most accurate description of what MockMvc simulates when a test calls mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))?
options: It calls the matching controller method directly via reflection, bypassing DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping entirely.

It sends the request through the real DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, argument resolvers, and HttpMessageConverters, but without opening an actual network socket or starting a real servlet container.
It sends a genuine HTTP request over the loopback network interface to a lightweight, temporary embedded server.
It replaces the controller with a Mockito-generated stub that returns a hardcoded response.
assessments.explanation: MockMvc dispatches the simulated request through Spring MVC's real machinery end to end -- routing, binding, conversion, validation, and exception handling all genuinely execute -- with the sole simplification being that no real network socket or servlet container thread is involved. Option A is wrong because routing and binding genuinely occur through HandlerMapping and argument resolvers, not direct reflection. Option C describes what TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient do against a real embedded server (as with @SpringBootTest's RANDOM_PORT), not MockMvc. Option D is wrong -- the controller itself is real and unmocked; only its own dependencies (like a @Service) would be mocked, and only if you explicitly did so.

assessments.prompt: A test writes `jsonPath("$.items").value("mug")` against a response whose items field is a JSON array containing several strings, one of which is "mug". What happens?
options: The assertion passes, because .value(...) automatically checks whether the given value is present anywhere in the array.

The assertion fails or produces a confusing type-mismatch error, because .value(...) expects the JSONPath expression to resolve to a single scalar, not a collection -- jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("mug") for a specific index, or jsonPath("$.items", hasItem("mug")) for membership, are the corrections.
The assertion silently passes regardless of the array's actual contents, because a path with no index is treated as an automatic wildcard match.
Spring MVC automatically converts the array into just its first element before the comparison runs.
assessments.explanation: The module calls out this exact mistake: asserting .value(...) against a jsonPath expression that resolves to an array (rather than a single scalar) produces a confusing failure, because .value(...) expects a scalar match. The two corrections it names directly are indexing into a specific element (jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("mug")) or using a Hamcrest membership matcher against the whole collection (jsonPath("$.items", hasItem("mug"))), depending on what's actually intended. Options A, C, and D each describe automatic, forgiving behavior that jsonPath's .value(...) assertion does not actually provide.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes MockMvc from TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient?
options: MockMvc and TestRestTemplate are functionally identical; choosing between them is purely a matter of style.

TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient fire genuine HTTP requests at a real, running embedded server (typically paired with @SpringBootTest's RANDOM_PORT), exercising the whole stack including real network serialization; MockMvc simulates the same dispatch entirely in memory, with no real socket, testing the web layer's logic without paying for a network round trip.
MockMvc only supports GET requests -- POST, PUT, and DELETE require switching to TestRestTemplate.
TestRestTemplate cannot handle JSON responses at all, only plain text bodies.
assessments.explanation: The module draws this distinction explicitly: TestRestTemplate and WebTestClient are genuine end-to-end tools that need a real running server (the RANDOM_PORT style of @SpringBootTest seen in the previous concept), while MockMvc simulates the same dispatch machinery without any real socket, at unit-test-adjacent speed. Option A collapses a distinction the module treats as meaningful and load-bearing for choosing between them. Option C is false -- MockMvc fully supports post(...), put(...), and delete(...) via MockMvcRequestBuilders, as shown throughout this concept's own examples. Option D is false -- TestRestTemplate handles JSON responses just as readily as MockMvc does.

assessments.prompt: A response body contains the JSON key "customerName", but a test asserts `jsonPath("$.CustomerName").value("Amy")` (capital C). What happens?
options: The assertion passes, because JSONPath expressions are case-insensitive by default when matching JSON keys.

The assertion fails to find a matching value, because JSON keys -- and therefore the JSONPath expressions that navigate them -- are case-sensitive; $.CustomerName does not refer to the same field as $.customerName.
Spring MVC normalizes JSON key casing automatically before any jsonPath expression is evaluated against the response.
The test fails to compile, because jsonPath expressions are validated against the target DTO class's exact field names at compile time.
assessments.explanation: The module names JSON key case-sensitivity directly as a common source of jsonPath friction: $.items[0].name and $.items[0].Name are explicitly called out as different expressions, precisely because JSON keys are case-sensitive and jsonPath navigates them literally. Option A and C both invent a normalization step that doesn't exist. Option D is wrong -- jsonPath expressions are plain strings evaluated at runtime against the parsed response; there is no compile-time validation against a DTO's field names.

assessments.prompt: Explain, end to end, what happens when a MockMvc test calls mockMvc.perform(post(...).contentType(...).content(...)) against a @WebMvcTest-loaded controller that has a @MockBean service dependency, through to the final assertions.
assessments.modelAnswer: When perform(...) is called, MockMvc hands the simulated request to the real DispatcherServlet that was loaded as part of the @WebMvcTest context, exactly as a genuine HTTP request would be handled in production -- the only difference is that this request never actually traveled over a network socket. DispatcherServlet consults the HandlerMapping built at context startup to find the controller method whose path pattern and HTTP method match the request, using the declared Content-Type to help select an HttpMessageConverter capable of reading the request body -- for a JSON body, that's the autoconfigured Jackson converter. That converter deserializes the raw bytes into the target @RequestBody parameter's Java type, populating its fields from the JSON exactly as it would for a real request; if a @Valid annotation is present, Bean Validation then runs against that freshly-constructed object, and a violation short-circuits everything from this point forward, routing instead to whatever @ExceptionHandler is registered for validation failures. Assuming validation passes, the controller method's body actually executes -- and because the controller's @Service dependency was registered as a @MockBean rather than a real bean, any call into that service returns whatever behavior was stubbed via given(...)/when(...), or Mockito's silent default (null, 0, or an empty collection) if nothing was stubbed for that particular call. Whatever the controller method returns is then passed back through the same Jackson converter in reverse, serialized into the JSON response body that the andExpect(...) assertions inspect via status(), jsonPath(...), and similar matchers. Every one of these steps genuinely executes real Spring MVC code -- routing, conversion, validation, serialization -- which is exactly why a MockMvc test is a meaningful test of the web layer's actual behavior, not merely a check that a method returns a particular value.

concepts.title: Mocking Dependencies with @MockBean
concepts.description: @MockBean replaces a real bean in the Spring test context with a Mockito mock, letting a test isolate the component it actually cares about from its collaborators -- but that replacement has real consequences for what gets stubbed, what silently returns null, and how efficiently the test suite can reuse cached contexts.
learningObjectives: Explain what @MockBean does to the Spring test ApplicationContext, and how that differs from a plain Mockito mock created with @Mock or mock(...).
Stub a @MockBean's behavior with when(...).thenReturn(...) (or given(...).willReturn(...)) and verify interactions with verify(...).
Predict what an unstubbed @MockBean method call returns for object, primitive, and collection return types.
Explain why adding or removing a @MockBean can force Spring's test-context cache to build a brand-new context, and the performance implication of that.
Choose correctly between @MockBean and a hand-constructed fake for a given testing scenario.

sections.heading: What @MockBean Actually Replaces
sections.body:
`@MockBean`, applied to a field in a Spring test class, does two things at once: it creates a Mockito mock of the declared type, and it registers that mock *into the test's ApplicationContext*, replacing any real bean of that type that would otherwise have been there (or supplying one, in a slice like `@WebMvcTest`, where no real bean of that type was ever going to be registered in the first place). Every other bean in that context that depends on the mocked type -- most commonly, a controller depending on a service -- now receives the mock when the container wires it, exactly as it would receive a real bean.

This is a genuinely different mechanism from a plain Mockito mock created with `@Mock` (from `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`) or a direct call to `mock(SomeType.class)`. A plain Mockito mock is just a Java object you construct and wire in yourself, by hand, with no Spring container involved at all -- appropriate for a pure unit test of, say, a service class instantiated with `new OrderService(mockRepository)`. `@MockBean` specifically exists for the case where *Spring's own container* is responsible for constructing the object under test (a controller inside a `@WebMvcTest`, for instance) and you need the container itself to hand that object a mock instead of a real dependency, because you have no `new` call of your own to inject one into manually.

sections.heading: Stubbing and Verifying
sections.body: Once a `@MockBean` is registered, it behaves like an ordinary Mockito mock for the rest of the test: `given(mockedService.findById(1L)).willReturn(order)` (BDDMockito style) or the equivalent `when(mockedService.findById(1L)).thenReturn(order)` (plain Mockito style) tells the mock what to return for that specific call, and `willThrow(...)`/`thenThrow(...)` tells it to throw an exception instead -- useful for testing how a controller handles a failure from its service. After the code under test has run, `verify(mockedService).findById(1L)` asserts that the mock's `findById` method really was called with that exact argument; `verify(mockedService, times(2))....` asserts an exact call count; and `verify(mockedService).save(argThat(order -> order.getCustomerName().equals("Amy")))` verifies a call happened with an argument matching a custom predicate, useful when the passed object doesn't have a meaningful `equals()` implementation to compare against directly.

sections.heading: Default Mock Behavior and the Silent Null Trap
sections.body:
It's essential to know precisely what happens when a `@MockBean`'s method is called *without* having been stubbed for that particular call: Mockito does **not** throw an exception to flag the oversight. By default, it returns a lenient, type-appropriate default: `null` for any object return type, `0`/`0.0`/`false` for primitives, and an empty (but non-null) collection for many common collection return types, thanks to Mockito's built-in 'smart null' and default-answer behavior for those cases.

This matters because it's a genuinely common, quiet source of test bugs: if you stub `orderService.findById(1L)` but the controller under test actually calls `orderService.findById(2L)` (perhaps due to a real bug in the controller, extracting the wrong path variable), the mock doesn't complain about receiving an argument it wasn't told to expect -- it just silently returns `null` for that unstubbed call, and the resulting `NullPointerException` (if the controller then calls a method on that `null`) can look, at first glance, like a completely unrelated bug, when the real problem is a mismatch between what you stubbed and what actually got called. This is a real, contrasting difference from a genuinely unimplemented real bean, which would either not exist at all (a compile error or `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`) or throw a meaningful domain exception -- an unstubbed mock fails *silently and generically* instead, which is precisely why it's worth stubbing every call path a test actually exercises, not just the 'happy path' you're most focused on.

sections.heading: @MockBean and Context Caching
sections.body:
As covered in this module's first concept, Spring's test framework caches a built `ApplicationContext` and reuses it across test classes that request an identical configuration, specifically to avoid re-paying a context's startup cost for every single test class. The set of `@MockBean`s declared on a test class is part of what defines that configuration's cache key -- two test classes that are otherwise identical but declare a *different* set of mocked beans are, from the cache's point of view, asking for two genuinely different contexts, and each gets its own freshly-built one.

This has a subtle, real-world performance implication worth knowing: a codebase where every test class mocks a slightly different, ad hoc combination of dependencies ends up defeating context caching far more often than one where test classes in the same area of the codebase consistently mock the same, shared set of collaborators (often by extending a common base test class that declares the standard set of `@MockBean`s for that layer). It's not a reason to avoid `@MockBean` -- it remains the right tool for isolating a component from its collaborators -- but it is a reason to keep the set of mocked beans within a given test class deliberate and, where reasonable, consistent with sibling test classes covering the same layer, rather than mocking an arbitrary, ever-changing subset per test method.

examples.title: Stubbing a @MockBean's Return Value
examples.explanation: @MockBean registers a Mockito mock as the OrderService bean inside this @WebMvcTest context, so OrderController's constructor is satisfied with the mock rather than a real service. given(...).willReturn(...) stubs exactly one call -- findById(1L) -- and the controller's real routing and JSON-serialization logic determines what actually ends up in the HTTP response, based on whatever the mock hands back. verify(orderService).findById(1L) is a separate, additional assertion from the jsonPath checks: it confirms the controller actually called the service with the expected argument, rather than only checking that the final response happened to look correct by some other path.

examples.title: Verifying Interactions and Argument Matching
examples.explanation: times(1) makes the expected call count explicit rather than assuming a bare verify(...) (which also defaults to exactly once) is self-evidently correct -- useful when a test's whole point is confirming a side-effecting operation like a delete happens exactly once, not zero times and not accidentally twice. The second verify, with never() and an argThat predicate for any id other than 42, adds a negative assertion: it would fail if the controller somehow called deleteById with a different id at any point during the test, catching a subtly wrong implementation that only checking the positive case might miss.

examples.title: The Silent-Null Trap From an Unstubbed Call
examples.explanation: This example is deliberately about what goes wrong, not a passing test: because the mock was only stubbed for findById(1L), a controller bug that calls findById(0L) instead receives Mockito's silent default of null for that unstubbed call -- no exception, no warning. The NullPointerException that follows happens later, wherever the controller (or the JSON serializer) tries to use that null Order, which can be a confusing distance away from the real defect. The lesson is procedural: when a MockMvc test produces an unexpected 500 error instead of a clean assertion failure, checking whether every call the code under test actually makes was genuinely stubbed -- not just the one you assumed it would make -- is one of the first, most productive places to look.

misconceptions.description: @MockBean is exactly the same as a plain Mockito @Mock or mock(...) call -- just a different-sounding annotation for creating a mock object.
misconceptions.clarification: Both create a genuine Mockito mock underneath, but @MockBean additionally registers that mock INTO Spring's ApplicationContext, replacing (or supplying) the bean of that type for every other bean the container wires -- which only matters, and only makes sense, when Spring's own container is responsible for constructing the object under test. A plain @Mock or mock(...) call produces an object you wire in yourself, entirely outside any Spring container, appropriate for a pure unit test built with `new`. Using @MockBean when no Spring context is involved at all is unnecessary; using a plain Mockito mock when you actually need Spring's container to inject that mock into another bean it's constructing (like a controller in a @WebMvcTest) simply won't work, since there's no `new` call of your own to hand the mock to.

misconceptions.description: If you forget to stub a @MockBean's method before it gets called during a test, Mockito throws an exception to warn you that the call was unexpected.
misconceptions.clarification: Mockito's default behavior for an unstubbed mock method call is lenient, not strict: it silently returns null for object return types, a primitive's zero-equivalent (0, 0.0, false) for primitive return types, and an empty collection for many common collection return types -- with no exception and no warning printed anywhere. This is exactly why an unstubbed call that the test didn't anticipate tends to surface later as a confusing NullPointerException somewhere downstream, rather than as an immediate, clearly-labeled test failure at the point the unexpected call actually happened.

exercises.prompt: This test fails with a NullPointerException thrown from inside OrderController, not from the test method itself. Given that OrderController.getOrder(id) calls orderService.findById(id) and then calls .getCustomerName() on the result, find and fix the bug in the test.
hints: Look carefully at the id used in the stub (given(orderService.findById(2L))) versus the id in the actual request path (/api/orders/1).
The mock was only told what to do for findById(2L). What does it do when the controller actually calls findById(1L) instead?
Fix either the stub's argument or the request path so they refer to the same order id -- they currently disagree.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The request in this test hits GET /api/orders/1, which causes the controller to call orderService.findById(1L) -- but the stub was written for findById(2L), a completely different, unstubbed call as far as Mockito is concerned. Because Mockito's default behavior for an unstubbed call is to silently return null rather than throw or warn, orderService.findById(1L) returned null, and the controller's own attempt to call .getCustomerName() on that null Order threw the NullPointerException the test actually observed -- nowhere near the assertion lines, which never even got a chance to run. Changing the stub to findById(1L) (matching the actual request) makes the mock respond correctly to the call the controller genuinely makes, letting the rest of the test run and assert as intended.

exercises.prompt: Given a @MockBean InventoryService inventoryService with no stubbing configured for any of its methods, what does each of these calls return, and why don't any of them throw an exception?
exercises.code:
// No when(...)/given(...) stubbing has been set up for inventoryService at all.

Integer count = inventoryService.getStockCount("WIDGET");     // int return type
String name = inventoryService.getProductName("WIDGET");      // String return type
boolean inStock = inventoryService.isInStock("WIDGET");        // boolean return type
List<String> tags = inventoryService.getTags("WIDGET");        // List<String> return type
hints: Mockito's default, unstubbed behavior differs by the DECLARED RETURN TYPE of the method, not by whether the method 'makes sense' to call.
Primitive return types (int, boolean) have a natural zero-equivalent default; reference types like String default to something else entirely.
Many common collection return types (List, Set, Map) get a smart default too, rather than defaulting the same way a plain object reference would.
exercises.expectedAnswer: count is 0 (int's default), name is null (String is a reference type with no stubbing), inStock is false (boolean's default), and tags is an empty List (Mockito's smart default for common collection return types) -- none of these calls throw, because Mockito's default answer for an unstubbed mock method is a lenient, type-appropriate default value, not an exception.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Mockito assigns a default 'answer' to every mock method that hasn't been explicitly stubbed, and that default depends entirely on the method's declared return type. For primitive numeric and boolean return types, the default is the type's natural zero-equivalent -- 0 for getStockCount's int, false for isInStock's boolean -- because a primitive can't be null and Mockito has to return something. For an ordinary reference type like String, with no special-cased default behavior, the answer is null. For well-known collection interfaces like List, Set, and Map, Mockito's default answer (RETURNS_DEFAULTS, which delegates to ReturnsEmptyValues) specifically returns an empty, non-null collection rather than null, precisely to reduce a common and easy-to-hit source of NullPointerExceptions when calling .size() or iterating over an unstubbed collection result. None of these calls throw an exception at all, which is exactly the behavior worth internalizing: a genuinely unanticipated call to a @MockBean fails silently and by returning something plausible-looking, not loudly.

assessments.prompt: A @MockBean UserRepository has no stubbing configured for its findByEmail(String) method, which returns Optional<User>. A test calls repository.findByEmail("amy@example.com") without stubbing it first. What is returned?
options: The method throws NullPointerException immediately, because Mockito requires every mock method to be explicitly stubbed before it's called.
An empty Optional (Optional.empty()), because Mockito's default answer recognizes Optional as a special case and avoids returning a bare null for it.
A real UserRepository bean is used instead, since @MockBean falls back to the actual implementation for unstubbed methods.
The test fails to compile, because calling an unstubbed mock method is a Mockito error caught at compile time.
assessments.explanation: Mockito's default answer behavior includes a specific case for Optional-returning methods: rather than returning a bare null (which would be an especially easy source of confusing NullPointerExceptions given how often Optional is chained with .map()/.orElse()), it returns Optional.empty() by default when a method returning Optional hasn't been stubbed. Option A is wrong -- Mockito never requires stubbing before a call; it always has SOME default answer ready. Option C is wrong -- @MockBean fully replaces the real bean; there is no fallback to a real implementation for calls that weren't stubbed. Option D is wrong -- there's nothing about an unstubbed call that Mockito or the compiler can detect statically; it's a purely runtime behavior.

assessments.prompt: A pure unit test constructs `OrderService service = new OrderService(mockRepository);` directly, with no Spring container involved anywhere in the test. What is the more appropriate way to create mockRepository, and why?
options: @MockBean, since it is always the preferred, more modern replacement for creating any mock in a Spring Boot codebase.

A plain Mockito mock, created via @Mock or mock(OrderRepository.class), because no Spring container is constructing OrderService here -- the mock just needs to be an ordinary Java object handed directly into the constructor, and @MockBean's whole reason for existing (registering into an ApplicationContext) has nothing to attach to.
Either approach works identically, since @MockBean is simply a more verbose alias for a plain mock(...) call.
Neither -- OrderRepository must be a genuine bean retrieved from a real ApplicationContext for this test to be considered valid.
assessments.explanation: The deciding factor is who constructs the object under test: here, the test itself calls `new OrderService(...)` directly, so there's no Spring container in the picture at all for @MockBean's context-registration behavior to do anything useful with -- a plain Mockito mock is simply an ordinary object the test wires in by hand. Option A overgeneralizes @MockBean's purpose to situations where it provides no benefit. Option C is false -- @MockBean does real, extra work (registering into an ApplicationContext) that a plain mock does not, even though both produce a genuine Mockito mock underneath. Option D invents a requirement that contradicts the entire point of writing a pure, Spring-free unit test.

assessments.prompt: A @MockBean has three unstubbed methods: getTags() returning List<String>, getDescription() returning String, and isActive() returning boolean. Which of these calls is most likely to eventually cause a NullPointerException downstream, if the calling code doesn't explicitly check for null first?
options: getTags(), because Mockito returns a bare null for List return types, exactly like any other reference type.

getDescription(), because String has no special-cased default in Mockito's default answer, so it returns null -- unlike getTags() (which receives Mockito's smart, empty-collection default) and isActive() (which receives boolean's false default).
isActive(), because Mockito cannot produce a default value for a primitive boolean return type and throws an exception instead.
None of them -- Mockito always throws UnsupportedStubbingException for any call that wasn't explicitly stubbed.
assessments.explanation: Mockito's default-answer behavior is type-aware: common collection interfaces like List get a smart, non-null empty-collection default specifically to avoid this exact class of bug, and primitives like boolean always have a natural zero-equivalent (false) to fall back on -- but an ordinary reference type like String has no such special case, so it defaults to a bare null, which is exactly the value most likely to blow up later if something calls a method on it without a null check. Option A misapplies the plain-reference-type default to List, which Mockito special-cases. Option C invents an exception Mockito does not throw for primitives. Option D is false generally -- Mockito's default behavior for unstubbed calls is a lenient default value, not an exception.

assessments.prompt: Two @WebMvcTest classes test different controllers but declare the exact same set of @MockBean types. A third test class in the same slice adds one additional @MockBean beyond what the other two declare. What is the effect on Spring's test-context caching?
options: All three test classes always share a single cached context regardless of their declared @MockBean sets, simply because they're all @WebMvcTest.

The first two test classes' identical configuration lets them share one cached context; the third class's different set of mocked beans counts as a different configuration, triggering a separate, freshly-built context instead of reuse.
Declaring any @MockBean at all permanently disables context caching for the remainder of the test run.
Spring merges all three test classes' configurations into one shared context containing every @MockBean declared across all of them.
assessments.explanation: The set of @MockBean types declared on a test class is explicitly part of what defines a configuration's cache key -- two test classes with an identical set of mocked beans can share a cached context, but a test class declaring even one additional mocked bean is, from the cache's perspective, requesting a genuinely different configuration, and gets its own freshly-built context rather than reusing the other two's. Option A ignores that cache keys are configuration-specific, not just annotation-specific. Option C overstates the effect -- @MockBean usage doesn't disable caching outright, it just needs to match exactly for reuse to happen. Option D describes a merging behavior Spring's test-context caching does not perform; contexts are reused wholesale when identical, never combined across differing configurations.

assessments.prompt: A teammate is confused about when to reach for @MockBean versus a plain Mockito mock created with new MockitoAnnotations/@Mock in a test with no Spring involved at all. Explain the distinction, and also explain the 'silent null' risk that comes with using any Mockito mock, @MockBean or not.
assessments.modelAnswer: The deciding question is who constructs the object under test. If a test builds the object under test itself, directly, with `new SomeService(dependencyA, dependencyB)`, then it's entirely the test's own responsibility to decide what to pass for each dependency -- and a plain Mockito mock, created with @Mock (combined with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) or a direct mock(SomeType.class) call, is exactly the right tool, because there's no Spring container involved in constructing SomeService at all; the mock is just an ordinary Java object handed directly into the constructor. @MockBean solves a different problem: it's for when SPRING's own container is the one constructing the object under test -- most commonly a controller inside a @WebMvcTest, which the container builds by inspecting its constructor and injecting whatever beans satisfy each parameter. Since the test has no `new` call of its own to inject a plain mock into, @MockBean tells the container itself to register a mock as the bean of that type, so it gets wired into the controller (or any other Spring-managed bean depending on it) the same way a real bean would be. Regardless of which mechanism produced the mock, the same underlying risk applies: Mockito's default behavior for any method call that wasn't explicitly stubbed is to return a lenient, type-appropriate default -- null for object types, a primitive's zero-equivalent for primitives, empty collections or Optional.empty() for several well-known container types -- rather than throwing an exception to flag that the call was unanticipated. This means a mismatch between what a test actually stubbed and what the code under test actually calls (a wrong argument, an extra unexpected invocation) doesn't fail loudly and immediately at the point of the mismatch; it fails quietly, producing a plausible-looking default value that often only causes a visible failure later, once something tries to use that value in a way that a null or a zero doesn't tolerate -- frequently a NullPointerException some distance away from the actual root cause. The practical takeaway is to stub every call path the code under test genuinely exercises during a given test, not just the one the test author had in mind, and to treat an unexpected NullPointerException surfacing from inside the code under test (rather than from the test's own assertions) as a strong hint to check whether a mock call actually matches what was stubbed.
